fact: Linus Torvalds began developing the Linux kernel in 1991 while he was a student at the University of Helsinki.
The Linux kernel is written primarily in C, with architecture-specific assembly and other supporting languages and tools.
Tux was created as the Linux penguin mascot artwork by Larry Ewing. The story that Linus Torvalds was bitten by a penguin is an anecdote, not a proven explanation for the mascot choice.
All 500 systems in the June 2026 TOP500 list were classified in the Linux operating-system family.
The first Linux kernel release, version 0.01, dates to September 1991.
Linux is technically the kernel; a Linux distribution combines the kernel with user-space tools, libraries, applications and package-management choices.

The name Linux is commonly explained as a blend of Linus and Unix, although the naming history is more nuanced: Linus initially used the name Freax, and the name Linux became established through the project's early hosting arrangements.
Android is built on the Linux kernel, which provides core services such as threading and low-level memory management.
The /proc filesystem is a virtual interface to information about running processes and kernel data; it is not an ordinary disk directory.
Linux is widely used in cloud servers, containers and embedded devices.
The /sys filesystem (sysfs) exposes information about kernel objects and the device model to user space.
Linux network namespaces can isolate network devices, protocol stacks, routing tables, firewall rules and port-number spaces.
Linux namespaces make global resources appear isolated to processes inside a namespace; containers use namespaces as one of their building blocks.
Linux control groups (cgroups) organize processes into hierarchies and provide interfaces for managing and accounting for resource use.

eBPF lets programs run in a constrained environment in the Linux kernel for tasks such as tracing, networking and security instrumentation, without changing kernel source code or loading a kernel module.
Linux capabilities split traditional superuser privileges into smaller permissions, such as CAP_NET_ADMIN and CAP_SYS_MODULE.
The Linux Security Module framework provides hooks used by security systems such as SELinux and AppArmor.
The ext4 filesystem uses a journal to help protect filesystem metadata from inconsistencies after a crash.
In ext4's default data=ordered mode, metadata is journaled and associated data blocks are written before the metadata transaction is committed; ordinary file data is not fully journaled by default.
Linux initramfs is an early userspace archive unpacked during boot; its /init program can locate and mount the real root filesystem.
GNU GRUB is a bootloader: it helps load an operating system kernel, but it is not the Linux kernel itself.
The Linux kernel supports multiple preemption models; the available choices depend on kernel configuration and architecture.
Linux's epoll API lets an application monitor many file descriptors for I/O readiness, using edge-triggered or level-triggered notification.
On Linux, fork() uses copy-on-write memory pages, so parent and child initially share physical pages until a write requires a copy.
The /proc/self path refers to the process accessing it, making it a convenient way for a process to inspect its own proc information.
Linux exposes kernel boot parameters through /proc/cmdline on systems where procfs is mounted.
The /proc/PID/fd directory contains symbolic links representing the file descriptors opened by a process.
The /proc/PID/maps file reports a process's mapped memory regions, including address ranges and permissions.
The Linux kernel provides the virtual filesystem layer (VFS), allowing user space to work with different filesystem implementations through common interfaces.
A Linux system can mount filesystems at different points in one directory tree; separate filesystems do not need separate drive-letter namespaces.
Linux supports loadable kernel modules, allowing supported kernel functionality such as drivers to be loaded or unloaded without rebuilding the entire kernel.
The dmesg command reads the kernel ring buffer, which commonly contains kernel and driver messages.
The uname command can report kernel-related system information, including the kernel release and machine architecture.
Linux process IDs (PIDs) identify processes within a PID namespace; PID namespaces allow containers to have their own PID numbering view.
Linux mount namespaces let processes have different views of the system's mount points.
Linux user namespaces allow processes to have different user and group ID mappings inside and outside the namespace.
Linux UTS namespaces isolate hostname and NIS domain-name identifiers.
Linux IPC namespaces isolate interprocess-communication resources such as System V IPC objects and POSIX message queues.
A network interface can belong to one network namespace at a time; virtual Ethernet pairs can connect network namespaces.
Linux supports seccomp filters, which can restrict the system calls a process is allowed to make.
The CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE capability allows a process to bind Internet-domain sockets to privileged ports below 1024.
The CAP_SYS_MODULE capability controls loading and unloading kernel modules.
The Linux kernel's /dev interface contains device nodes through which user-space programs can access device drivers.
Linux supports many processor architectures; the kernel source tree contains architecture-specific code under arch/.
The Linux kernel has a scheduler that chooses which runnable task gets CPU time; scheduling behavior is affected by policy and priority.
Linux provides real-time scheduling policies in addition to its normal scheduling policy classes.
The Linux kernel exports many tunable parameters through sysctl interfaces, commonly exposed under /proc/sys.
The Linux kernel's /proc/interrupts file reports interrupt counts by CPU and interrupt source.
The /proc/meminfo file reports memory statistics maintained by the Linux kernel.
The /proc/uptime file reports how long the system has been running and the amount of time spent idle.
Linux supports kernel tracing and performance tools such as ftrace and perf for observing kernel and system behavior.
eBPF programs can attach to networking and tracing-related kernel hooks, making eBPF useful for observability and performance analysis.
Linux supports multiple filesystem types, including ext4, XFS and Btrfs; the choice depends on workload and required features.
Linux's kernel command line can be used to pass parameters to the kernel and, depending on the parameter, to built-in components or early userspace.
The kernel's init process is the first user-space process started during a normal Linux boot and is assigned PID 1 in the initial PID namespace.
Linux can use a virtual memory mechanism called swap, which provides backing storage for memory pages that are not currently kept in RAM.
Linux supports hard links: multiple directory entries can refer to the same inode on a filesystem that supports them.
On Linux, pipes provide a unidirectional byte stream that allows processes to pass data to one another.
Linux signals provide a mechanism for notifying processes that an event has occurred; signals include SIGTERM, SIGKILL and SIGCHLD.
The Linux kernel can expose device and kernel-object relationships through sysfs, usually mounted at /sys.
io_uring is an asynchronous I/O interface introduced in Linux 5.1 that uses shared memory submission and completion rings to reduce syscall overhead.
The Linux Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer selects and terminates processes when the system runs critically low on physical memory and swap.
Linux transparent hugepages (THP) allow the kernel to automatically allocate 2MB or larger memory pages to reduce TLB misses.
The Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) served as the default Linux desktop/server task scheduler from kernel 2.6.23 until it was replaced by EEVDF in kernel 6.6.
EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First) replaced CFS in Linux 6.6 to improve latency responsiveness for interactive workloads.
The /dev/null device discards all data written to it while returning an end-of-file (EOF) status on read attempts.
The /dev/zero character device supplies an endless stream of null bytes (0x00) to any process reading from it.
/dev/urandom generates non-blocking pseudorandom numbers derived from the kernel entropy pool without blocking when entropy is low.
Since Linux 5.6, /dev/random and /dev/urandom behave identically under normal conditions after the initial entropy seed is established.
The Linux vDSO (virtual dynamic shared object) exports kernel space functions to user space to allow fast syscalls like gettimeofday without context switching.
OverlayFS is a union filesystem for Linux that allows two directory trees to be combined into one, forming the foundation of Docker image layers.
In Linux file permissions, the SUID bit on an executable causes the program to execute with the file owner's privileges instead of the calling user's privileges.
The Sticky Bit on a Linux directory ensures that files within that directory can only be deleted or renamed by their respective owners or root.
Linux netfilter is the underlying framework inside the kernel that provides packet filtering, NAT, and packet mangling used by iptables and nftables.
nftables is the modern successor to iptables, offering a unified user-space utility and simpler kernel packet evaluation syntax.
The Linux kernel uses swapiness (vm.swappiness) to balance between swapping out anonymous memory pages and dropping filesystem page cache.
KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine) converts the Linux kernel into a bare-metal hypervisor via hardware virtualization extensions (Intel VT-x / AMD-V).
Zram creates compressed block devices inside RAM that act as ultra-fast swap devices or temporary storage.
Systemd is an init system and system manager that uses socket activation and parallel service execution to speed up Linux boot times.
The /etc/fstab file defines static information regarding filesystems, mount points, and mount options processed during system boot.
udev is the dynamic device manager for the Linux kernel, responsible for creating nodes in /dev when hardware is connected or disconnected.
Linux signals SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP (19) cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored by standard process code.
A zombie process in Linux has completed execution via exit() but retains an entry in the process table until its parent reads its exit status via wait().
An orphan process is a Linux process whose parent has finished or died; orphan processes are automatically adopted by PID 1 (init/systemd).
Btrfs (B-tree FS) is a copy-on-write filesystem for Linux that supports built-in RAID, dynamic volume management, and instant snapshotting.
XFS is a high-performance 64-bit journaling filesystem developed by SGI and now widely used as default storage on enterprise Linux distributions.
Linux memory overcommit allows the kernel to allocate more virtual memory to processes than physical RAM and swap combined.
The Linux kernel source code repository migrated to Git in 2005 after Linus Torvalds created Git specifically for kernel development.
The /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches interface allows administrators to manually liberate page cache, dentries, and inodes from physical RAM.
Linux sysrq key shortcuts allow emergency low-level commands to be sent directly to the kernel, even during total system freezes.
The REISUB magic sysrq sequence safely unmounts filesystems, syncs data, and restarts a frozen Linux machine.
WireGuard is an extremely lightweight VPN protocol integrated directly into the Linux kernel starting with version 5.6.
Linux uses Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) to randomize memory address locations of key data areas to prevent buffer overflow attacks.
SELinux was originally developed by the United States National Security Agency (NSA) and released to the open-source community under GPL.
AppArmor relies on pathnames to enforce access rules, whereas SELinux relies on security labels (inodes and contexts).
The Linux command 'strace' intercepts and records system calls made by a process and the signals received by that process.
The Linux command 'lsof' lists information about files opened by processes, including disk files, named pipes, network sockets, and devices.
The /proc/cpuinfo virtual file exposes detailed CPU flags, architecture information, core counts, and CPU vendor identifiers.
Linux supports Control Groups version 2 (cgroups v2), which unifies resource hierarchies under a single tree layout.
Rust support was officially merged into the Linux kernel starting with Linux release 6.1.
Soft lockup kernel panics occur when a CPU task spends more than 20 seconds executing in kernel space without letting other tasks run.
Hard lockup kernel panics occur when a CPU fails to service local periodic timer interrupts for a prolonged period.
Linux uses POSIX Realtime Extensions to provide realtime priorities ranging from 1 to 99 under SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR.
The Linux kernel SCHED_DEADLINE policy implements the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithm for hard real-time tasks.
In Linux, symbolic links can span different filesystems, whereas hard links must exist on the same physical filesystem.
Linux page cache utilizes free RAM to store frequently accessed disk blocks, automatically freeing memory when applications require physical RAM.
The Linux 'nice' value adjusts a process priority level ranging from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest priority).
Linux supports Kernel Samepage Merging (KSM), allowing hypervisors to scan memory and merge identical memory pages into shared copy-on-write pages.
The Linux kernel utilizes a pseudo-filesystem named debugfs to expose debugging and profiling data to developers.
The kernel config file (.config) stores all feature flags, driver options, and architecture configurations chosen during kernel compilation.
Linux support for unified memory architecture (UMA) and Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) ensures efficient multi-socket CPU memory balancing.
Linux network interface bonding allows combining multiple physical network interfaces into a single virtual interface for redundancy or throughput.
The Linux Kernel Module loading utility 'modprobe' automatically resolves and loads module dependencies, unlike low-level 'insmod'.
The Linux environment variable PATH specifies a list of directories searched sequentially to locate command binaries.
GNU C Library (glibc) provides standard system calls and core wrapper functions used by most Linux userland applications.
musl is an alternative lightweight standard C library for Linux often used in minimal container environments like Alpine Linux.
Linux iptables features five default built-in tables: raw, filter, nat, mangle, and security.
The Linux kernel uses extended attributes (xattrs) to store arbitrary key-value metadata alongside files and directories.
LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup) is the standard platform-independent disk encryption format used by dm-crypt.
Linux devtmpfs mounts a virtual filesystem at /dev during early boot, presenting device nodes managed by the kernel core.
The Linux kernel uses the RCU (Read-Copy Update) synchronization mechanism to allow lockless read operations alongside concurrent writes.
The chroot system call changes the apparent root directory for the current running process and its child processes.
Systemd journals capture structured log messages from kernel space, early boot initramfs, and standard userspace services.
Linux tmpfs stores files in virtual memory using RAM and swap, providing high-speed storage that clears upon reboot.
The Linux kernel implements splice() system call to transfer data directly between file descriptors without copying data to user space.
Linux veth (virtual ethernet) devices act as connected pairs: packets sent into one end emerge at the opposite device end.
The Linux kernel exposes system uptime in seconds via the /proc/uptime virtual file.
Linux perf allows hardware performance counter monitoring, tracepoints, kprobes, and uprobes execution profiling.
The Linux 'sysctl' tool modifies kernel parameter configurations dynamically at runtime without requiring a kernel reboot.
SquashFS is a read-only compressed filesystem widely used for Linux live CDs, embedded devices, and container images.
Linux POSIX message queues allow asynchronous inter-process communication using structured messages with assigned priorities.
The kernel feature 'kexec' allows booting a new Linux kernel directly from a running kernel without undergoing hardware BIOS/UEFI resets.
Linux 'kdump' uses kexec to boot into a secondary rescue kernel to dump crash dumps (vmcore) when a primary kernel panic occurs.
The Linux security framework PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) allows system administrators to customize authentication mechanisms without editing source code.
Linux system call numbers differ across CPU architectures (e.g., x86_64 system call IDs differ from ARM64 system call IDs).
The inotify API provides mechanism for monitoring filesystem events such as file creation, modification, deletion, and movement.
fanotify is an advanced Linux filesystem notification API designed for malware scanning and hierarchical filesystem access monitoring.
Linux bridge virtual devices connect distinct Ethernet network segments together within software layer 2 forwarding.
The Linux 'ip' command from iproute2 replaces legacy utilities like 'ifconfig', 'route', and 'arp'.
The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) specifies standard locations for files and directories across Linux operating systems.
The /var directory in the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard stores variable state data, including system logs, databases, and spool files.
The /opt directory is designated by FHS for storing add-on application software packages.
Linux dynamic linkers (ld.so) load required shared libraries (.so files) when launching dynamically linked binaries.
The /etc/ld.so.conf configuration file and /etc/ld.so.cache binary index define search paths used by the dynamic linker.
The Linux kernel 'futex' (fast userspace mutex) provides fast locking by performing non-contended operations entirely in user space.
Linux namespaces were introduced incrementally, beginning with the mount namespace in Linux kernel version 2.4.19.
Linux supports Kernel Live Patching (KLP), enabling dynamic security fixes without restarting the core system kernel.
The Linux audit framework collects security-relevant event records maintained by kernel audit subsystem hooks.
The 'vmstat' command reports virtual memory statistics, CPU utilization, block I/O counts, and process activity snapshot summaries.
The 'iostat' utility monitors system input/output device loading by observing active physical disk hardware times.
Linux implements virtual memory swapping via page-granularity operations rather than swapping entire process memory structures.
In Linux filesystems, an inode stores metadata about a file (size, permissions, timestamps, block pointers) but does not store the file name.
Directory entries in Linux (dentries) map file names to their corresponding inode numbers.
Linux POSIX threads (NPTL - Native POSIX Thread Library) implement threads as task structs executed via the clone() system call.
The clone() system call in Linux provides fine-grained control over what resources (memory, file descriptors, signal handlers) are shared between parent and child.
Linux memory pages are typically 4KB in size on standard x86_64 architecture, though larger pages (2MB/1GB) are supported via HugeTLB.
The /proc/sys/fs/file-max file controls the maximum total number of open file handles allowed across the entire Linux system.
The ulimit command sets resource limits (open files, max processes, stack size) for the current shell and its child processes.
PAM configuration files reside in /etc/pam.d/ and define authentication rules for system services like sshd, sudo, and login.
Linux device major numbers identify the driver associated with a device, while minor numbers identify the specific device instance.
Block devices transfer data in fixed-size blocks and support random access, whereas character devices stream data sequentially byte-by-byte.
Linux dm-crypt is a transparent disk encryption subsystem operating at the block device layer within the Linux kernel.
Logical Volume Manager (LVM) allows flexible disk management including resizing physical volumes, volume groups, and logical volumes on the fly.
Linux network namespaces can be managed directly using the 'ip netns' command utility.
The /proc/net directory provides symbolic links and virtual files giving detailed insights into network protocols and active sockets.
Linux 'ss' tool retrieves socket statistics and displays TCP, UDP, and domain socket connections faster than legacy 'netstat'.
The Linux kernel implements TCP SYN cookies to mitigate TCP SYN flood denial-of-service attacks without allocating memory pools prematurely.
Systemd targets replace traditional SysV init runlevels with declarative service grouping constructs.
Linux 'journalctl' inspects logs generated by systemd-journald using custom filters like unit, priority, or time ranges.
The Linux kernel uses the anticipatory, deadline, or BFQ (Budget Fair Queueing) schedulers to manage disk block I/O requests.
Linux pressure stall information (PSI) monitors CPU, memory, and I/O resource scarcity metrics in real time.
The /sys/class directory organizes devices exposed by sysfs into functional categories such as net, block, sound, and power_supply.
Linux umask (user file-creation mode mask) subtracts default permissions when creating new files and directories.
Linux Access Control Lists (ACLs) provide fine-grained permissions beyond standard owner/group/other permission models.
The Linux 'getfacl' and 'setfacl' commands read and modify extended POSIX file access control entries.
Linux 'tar' (Tape Archiver) bundles multiple files into a single archive file without compressing unless combined with tools like gzip or xz.
The /proc/locks file lists all file locks currently held across the system by processes using flock or fcntl.
Linux supports user-space filesystems (FUSE), enabling non-privileged users to build virtual filesystems without compiling kernel code.
The Linux core dump feature saves process memory contents to disk when a process terminates abnormally due to a crash signal.
The /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern file configures core dump output file naming conventions or piping behaviors.
Linux 'chown' changes ownership of files or directories, while 'chgrp' specifically updates group ownership assignment.
The /etc/passwd file stores local user account parameters including username, UID, primary GID, home directory, and login shell.
The /etc/shadow file stores secure encrypted user password hashes inaccessible to non-privileged standard users.
Linux supports Kernel Control Flow Integrity (CFI) to defend against indirect function call redirection attacks.
Linux System V IPC includes shared memory segments, semaphore sets, and message queues accessible via sysvipc syscalls.
POSIX shared memory (shm_open) creates shared memory regions exposed under the /dev/shm tmpfs virtual directory.
Linux supports namespaces for time isolation (CLONE_NEWTIME), allowing containers to set virtual offset system clocks.
The /proc/cmdline file displays arguments passed from bootloaders to the Linux kernel during system initialization.
Linux 'tee' command reads from standard input and writes results simultaneously to both standard output and files.
The Linux command 'xargs' builds and executes command lines using input arguments passed from standard input streams.
Linux security module AppArmor stores configuration profiles under /etc/apparmor.d/.
Linux system call 'mmap' creates dynamic memory mappings in process address space backed by physical files or anonymous RAM.
The 'mprotect' system call sets or updates memory protection flags (READ, WRITE, EXECUTE) on mapped memory regions.
Linux memory protection key (pkeys) support allows userland applications to change access permissions of memory pages without invoking context switches.
Linux uses task structs to track all running tasks, managing process execution status, capabilities, memory maps, and open descriptors.
Linux namespaces can be joined by external processes using the 'setns()' system call.
The 'unshare()' system call allows a process to disassociate parts of its execution context without needing to fork a child process.
Linux exposes kernel configuration options at runtime via /proc/config.gz when CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC is enabled.
The Linux Landlock security module allows unprivileged processes to restrict their own file system access permissions securely.
The Linux kernel version naming scheme uses a version number format of Major.Minor.Patch (e.g., 6.6.12).
